STYLE: HAND-DRAWN INK AND WASH (for informal, thinking-aloud lessons; reflection; a sketchbook voice)
- A skilled illustrator's location sketch: perspective drawn by eye but sound, line drives the drawing, with real variation in weight and a slight natural wobble (no ruler-perfect lines, no shaky jitter either).
- Ink in lm-outline: the near objects in a 3 to 4 px line, the far wall in 1.5 px; lines overshoot slightly at corners; some edges are left open where the light hits.
- Wash in two or three transparent tones per material, laid loosely and not filling to the line everywhere; the paper (wall or paper colour) is left untouched where the light is strongest.
- Hatching or a darker wash only in the shadow side and under things.
- Work outside-in: the big silhouettes and the few large dark shapes first, detail last; one decisive line, not five; heavier lines on near objects, overlaps and the undersides of forms; the wash never repeats what the ink already says.
- Light: Light is the paper left white; shadow is a cool wash in the shadow colour at 0.2 to 0.3 opacity, with hatching in the deepest places.
- Texture: Paper fibres as sparse fine vector strokes in lm-texture; wash edges a little irregular (blooms) on 2 or 3 large areas.
- Depth: Far: thin line, almost no wash. Mid: line and wash. Near: the strongest line and the darkest wash.
- Quality bar: A page from a professional illustrator's sketchbook of a real office: loose, confident, specific.

THE WORLD: INSIDE THE BODY AND THE MICROSCOPIC
The inside of one healthy adult body, seen at true microscopic scale. Every set is a real tissue of the same body: the blood in a small artery, the skin on the back of a hand, the air sacs deep in the lungs, the lining of the large intestine, and a patch of the brain's outer layer. Each is drawn as a believable, softly lit place with the real shapes and the real relative sizes of what is there, simplified only by leaving out clutter: real tissue is packed far more densely than these sets show, and each scene says so.
Architecture:
- blood: red blood cells as biconcave discs about 7.5 micrometres across and about 2 micrometres thick at the rim (thinner in the dimpled centre), never spheres or doughnuts with a hole; white blood cells larger and round (a neutrophil about 12 micrometres) with a ruffled surface; platelets as small flat ovals 2 to 3 micrometres; the fluid (plasma) clear and pale straw-yellow
- vessel walls: lined with one layer of thin, flat cells (endothelium) elongated along the flow, each with an oval bulge where its nucleus sits, fitted together like long paving stones; the smallest vessels (capillaries) only 5 to 10 micrometres wide, so red cells pass in single file
- skin: the surface layer is a pavement of flat, many-sided dead cells (corneocytes) about 30 to 50 micrometres across and less than 1 micrometre thick, overlapping like roof tiles and lifting at their edges before they flake off; crossed by a diamond pattern of fine furrows; hairs about 75 micrometres thick rising from their openings with overlapping scales on the shaft; sweat duct openings about 20 to 50 micrometres across
- lungs: hundreds of millions of air sacs (alveoli), each about 200 micrometres across, opening off small ducts like the cells of a honeycomb; their walls very thin and filled with a dense net of capillaries; alveolar macrophages (cleaner cells about 20 micrometres across) crawling on the inner surface
- large intestine: a lining of tall column-shaped cells with a fuzzy top edge (the brush border), mucus-making goblet cells among them, and the openings of tube-shaped pits (crypts); above it a firm inner mucus layer, normally free of bacteria, and above that a looser outer mucus layer where the gut's bacteria live
- brain: neurons with cell bodies about 15 to 25 micrometres across, long branching dendrites studded with tiny spines (about 1 to 2 micrometres), one thin axon each, wrapped in places by a segmented fatty sheath (myelin) with small gaps; star-shaped support cells (astrocytes) touching the capillaries
Materials: wet, glossy, translucent living tissue: soft pinks, creams and reds, pale straw-yellow fluids, clear gels, a few cooler blues and violets in the brain and the lungs. Nothing is hard-edged or metallic. Palette families in this world (the set palette was named for rooms): fluids, mucus and the wet sheen on surfaces are glass; the main tissue surfaces and vessel walls are wall; a second tissue or a cell type that must read apart from the walls is fabric2; red blood cells and blood-filled capillaries are brick; white blood cells, macrophages and pale cells are paper; bacteria are plant; neurons and their branches are fabric; the deep background beyond the tissue is ceiling (for an enclosed, dark place) or sky (for an open, lit one); hair and keratin plates are wood; one small signal (a virus, a nerve impulse, a pollutant particle) is accent; a soft inner glow is light
Scale (draw to these real sizes; a person is about 1.75 m):
- 1 micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre; a human hair is about 75 micrometres thick
- a red blood cell is about 7.5 micrometres across; a capillary 5 to 10 micrometres; a neutrophil about 12; an alveolar macrophage about 20; a platelet 2 to 3
- a skin surface cell is 30 to 50 micrometres across; a common skin bacterium (a round coccus) about 1 micrometre; a gut bacterium (a rod) about 1 by 2 to 3 micrometres; a flu virus about 0.1 micrometre, too small to see at any scale used here
- an alveolus is about 200 micrometres across; a fine air pollution particle (PM2.5) is up to 2.5 micrometres
- a neuron's cell body is about 15 to 25 micrometres; a dendritic spine 1 to 2 micrometres; the colon's inner mucus layer about 100 micrometres thick (measurements range from 50 to 300)
- each scene states its own scale (pixels per micrometre) and keeps it for everything in the picture
Signs of life (every set shows someone works here):
- life in motion: cells caught mid-tumble, a white cell squeezing through a gap, bacteria dividing (one rod pinched in the middle), a cell flake lifting
- the body's work: oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood (brighter and darker red) in neighbouring vessels, mucus being made, a hair growing, a cleaner cell carrying a swallowed particle
- wear and repair: a damaged patch of lining being repaired, a skin flake curling away, a spent platelet clump
- traces from outside: a speck of dust in the lungs, a fibre of food in the gut, a smear of grime on the skin
Default light: There is no daylight inside the body. Every set uses a soft, even, warm-white light that seems to come through the thin tissue itself, brightest at the far opening or the centre of the space, so each surface shows a gentle glossy highlight on the side toward that glow and a soft translucent shade on the other; no hard cast shadows except small contact shadows where things touch.
Outside: There is no outside: each set is enclosed tissue or a space within it.
Motifs: Use at least three of these in every scene so the sets belong to one body (each scene names the ones its camera can see): biconcave red blood cells wherever blood shows, a fine capillary with red cells in single file, a wet glossy sheen on every surface, soft translucent tissue lit from within, tiny drifting specks in the fluid, the empty scale-bar slot in the lower right corner.

- red blood cell: a biconcave disc about 7.5 micrometres across: round in face view with a shallow dimple in the middle (darker there because it is thinner), about 2 micrometres thick at its rounded rim and about 1 micrometre at the centre, so edge-on it looks like a short dumbbell; smooth, glossy, red; no nucleus, no hole; flexible, so it bends when it squeezes past something

- platelet: a small flat oval about 2 to 3 micrometres long and less than 1 thick, pale straw to pale pink, smooth; a few stuck together in a small clump
- vessel lining: the inside wall of the vessel: one layer of thin, flat cells (endothelium) about 10 micrometres wide and 30 to 50 long, all elongated along the flow, fitted edge to edge like long paving stones with fine darker borders, each with a soft oval bulge where its nucleus sits; glossy and wet
- plasma: the fluid of the blood: clear and pale straw-yellow (never red), with a faint haze and a few tiny drifting specks
- scale bar: a plain horizontal line of a stated length in pixels with a short upright tick at each end, in the lower right corner, with an empty slot rect beside it for its label (no numbers drawn)
- skin surface cells: the dead flat cells (corneocytes) of the skin's surface: many-sided plates (mostly five or six sides) 30 to 50 micrometres across and less than 1 micrometre thick, overlapping like roof tiles in layers, their edges slightly raised; pale cream to beige, matte with a faint sheen
- skin furrows: the fine criss-cross lines of the skin: shallow valleys a few plates wide where the surface folds down, crossing in a diamond pattern, slightly shaded
- hair: a hair about 75 micrometres thick rising at an angle from a round opening ringed by raised plates: a long cylinder covered in overlapping, slightly lifted scales (the cuticle) like roof slates or a pine cone's surface, pale brown, glossy
- sweat duct opening: a small round opening about 40 micrometres across in the skin's surface (its size on the surface was not measured directly), with a slightly raised rim of plates, holding a clear, domed bead of sweat that reflects the light
- skin bacteria: skin bacteria: round cocci about 1 micrometre across in grape-like clusters of tens to hundreds, and a few small groups of short rods; pale green-grey and translucent, sitting in the furrows and around the hair
- air sac: an alveolus: a rounded, cup-shaped chamber about 200 micrometres across, open on one side to a small duct, sharing thin walls with its neighbours like the cells of a honeycomb; the walls pink, thin and translucent, with a wet film on their inner surface
- capillary net: a dense mesh of capillaries in the air sacs' walls: smooth tubes 6 to 8 micrometres wide joining and branching in a net, filled with red blood cells passing in single file and bending to fit
- alveolar macrophage: a cleaner cell about 20 micrometres across: irregular and pale, with ruffled, reaching edges and a few small dark particles visible inside it
- dust particles: fine particles of dust and soot: dark grey irregular specks 1 to 10 micrometres across (the finest, PM2.5, are up to 2.5 micrometres), some in small clumps
- airway: the end of a small airway (a bronchiole about 0.5 mm across): a round tunnel with a smooth, slightly ridged lining, darker and deeper than the air sacs
- gut lining cells: the lining of the large intestine: tall column-shaped cells about 25 micrometres tall and 6 to 8 wide standing side by side in one layer, each with an oval nucleus near its base and a fine, fuzzy brush border along its top
- goblet cells: mucus-making cells among the lining cells: the same height, but swollen at the top like a goblet, full of pale round mucus granules, releasing mucus from their tops
- crypts: the openings of the tube-shaped pits that dip down into the lining, each about 45 micrometres across, ringed by lining and goblet cells
- inner mucus layer: a firm, clear gel about 100 micrometres thick lying on the lining, very faintly layered in horizontal sheets, normally free of bacteria; slightly blue-grey and glossy
- outer mucus layer: a looser, cloudier gel above the inner layer where the gut's bacteria live
- gut bacteria: the gut's bacteria: rods about 1 micrometre wide and 2 to 3 long (some in short chains, a few with a thin whip-like tail), round cocci about 1 micrometre in pairs and clusters, and a few slightly curved forms; translucent green-grey with small highlights
- food fibres: fibres of digested plant food: pale, twisted, ribbon-like strands up to about 100 micrometres long, some frayed at the ends
- neuron: a pyramidal neuron: a cell body shaped like a rounded pyramid 15 to 25 micrometres tall with a pale round nucleus inside; one thick main dendrite rising from its tip and branching; several thinner dendrites spreading from its base, each branching and tapering; one thin axon leaving the base
- dendritic spines: tiny protrusions 1 to 2 micrometres long along the dendrites, of three kinds: thin ones, short stubby ones and mushroom-shaped ones with a round head on a narrow neck
- axon and myelin: the neuron's single thin output fibre, about 1 micrometre thick, wrapped in places by pale, pearly sausage-shaped sheaths (myelin) with small bare gaps (nodes) between them; it branches near its end into small knobs
- synapse: the meeting point of an axon's small swollen ending and a dendrite's spine, separated by a gap too narrow to see at this scale, drawn as a hairline with a faint glow
- astrocyte: a star-shaped support cell about 20 micrometres across with many fine, branching, slightly fuzzy arms, some ending in small flattened feet pressed against a capillary
- capillary: a small blood vessel about 7 micrometres wide, a smooth translucent tube with red blood cells inside it in single file
